claim: Taking a 30-year mortgage and paying it at the 15-year payment is not the same as a 15-year loan, because the 15-year rate is lower. At the latest weekly survey rates (30-year 7.03%, 15-year 6.42%, a 0.61-point gap), a borrower who pays the 15-year payment on a 30-year loan needs 193 months instead of 180 to finish and pays about $11,181 more interest per $100,000 borrowed. Across all 1,831 weeks since 1991 in which both rates were published, the gap averaged 0.575 points, was at least 0.50 points in 62.9% of weeks, and the median extra cost of this 'flexibility' was about $8,860 per $100,000. The flexibility of the lower required payment has a price, and this is history, not a forecast.

Weekly Freddie Mac PMMS averages MORTGAGE30US and MORTGAGE15US (percent) from data/, using only weeks present in both files (1991-08-30 through 2026-09-24). Premium for rates (r30, r15) on a $100,000 loan: P = 100000*i15/(1-(1+i15)^-180) with i15 = r15/1200 (the 15-year payment). 15-year interest = 180*P - 100000. Then amortize a 100000 balance at monthly rate i30 = r30/1200, paying P each month (final month pays the remaining balance*(1+i30)); 30-year-prepaid interest = total paid - 100000. Premium = 30-year-prepaid interest - 15-year interest, in dollars. Evaluated at r30=7.03, r15=6.42 (week 2026-09-24); rounded to the dollar.
Number of monthly payments (including the final partial one) needed to repay the 30-year loan at 7.03% when paying the 15-year payment computed at 6.42%, per the method in latest_premium_per_100k.

assumptions: Borrower's rates equal the national weekly survey averages for each term; points, fees and credit adjustments are ignored (both surveys report averages that include points paid).
Monthly compounding at annual rate/12; no taxes, no mortgage insurance, no refinancing, no missed or extra payments beyond the 15-year payment.
Dollar amounts are undiscounted totals of interest paid, per $100,000 of principal.
